units.title: Threat models for clients, services and operators, workload identity and mutual TLS
outcomes: Build a threat model across client, network, service, storage, operator, tenant, dependency and artifact boundaries, naming the trust boundary each threat crosses.
Assign SPIFFE IDs to workloads and explain what each side verifies during mutual TLS with X.509-SVIDs.
Check JWT time claims with inclusive not-before and exclusive expiration rules, and state what claim checks cannot cover.
units.why: Authorization, tenancy and audit all assume the caller is who it claims to be. A forged or stale identity makes every later check in this section decide on false input.

next.note: Enforce what an authenticated identity may do on every data path.
Protect the keys and credentials those identities use.

study.title: Threat model method: diagrams, trust boundaries, STRIDE
study.locator: System Modeling (data-flow diagrams, trust boundaries, data stores and processes); Threat Identification (the STRIDE table applied to components, data flows and trust boundaries); Response and Mitigations

study.title: mTLS and service identity: Zero Trust, handshake, SPIFFE
study.locator: The Zero Trust model; mTLS handshake mechanics; Certificate lifecycle: issuance, rotation, revocation; SPIFFE and SPIRE
study.depth: Skim Service mesh as the practical answer and When mTLS is overkill for tool choice. This unit builds on SPIFFE concepts, not on deploying a mesh.

study.title: SPIFFE Workload API: SVIDs, bundles and streaming updates
study.locator: X.509-SVID Profile: FetchX509SVID and FetchX509Bundles; Stream Responses (every message is a complete update that replaces prior state); Federated Bundles for cross-domain trust (page read 2026-10-15)

focus: Draw the data-flow diagram first, then apply STRIDE per boundary. A threat without a named crossing is a worry, not a model.
A SPIFFE ID names a trust domain plus a workload path, for example `spiffe://prod.example/log-writer`. The peer verifies the SVID signature against its trust bundle and then authorizes that ID.

Workload API responses replace prior state. An empty optional `federated_bundles` map removes previously supplied federated bundles; the local trust-domain bundle must always be present, and loss of all entitlement arrives as `PermissionDenied`. Clients hold the connection open and redial when it drops.
Caller identification at the endpoint is out-of-band attestation, not a client password. The API itself carries no direct client authentication.
units.reproduce: Without notes, write `spiffe://` IDs for three loglab processes in one trust domain, then state what each side checks during mutual TLS and what a client must do when its bundle stream delivers an empty optional federated-bundle map.
traps: Server-authenticated TLS alone does not authenticate the client workload. Use a client certificate or a separate verified application credential; cipher strength does not establish caller identity.
Merging streamed bundle updates instead of replacing them. A removed bundle that stays trusted is a revoked identity that still authenticates.
Treating claim checks as token verification. The JWT exercise states it plainly: structure and signature are assumed already verified, and revocation is out of scope.

selfTest.q: A forged client identity crosses the service boundary. Which STRIDE category is it, and what does it violate?
selfTest.a: Spoofing, which violates authentication. The fix sits at the trust boundary the forged identity crosses.

selfTest.q: When would a workload call `FetchX509Bundles` instead of `FetchX509SVID`?
selfTest.a: When it only needs bundles to validate peers, without obtaining its own SVID and private key. Both RPCs can supply local and federated bundles.

selfTest.q: A bundle stream delivers a message without the bundle for `spiffe://peer.example`. What must the client do?
selfTest.a: Unload that bundle. Responses are complete updates, so absence is a redaction, and peers presenting those SVIDs must no longer verify.

selfTest.q: `isValid` accepts `iat=10, nbf=10, exp=20` at `now=10` but rejects it at `now=20`. Why?
selfTest.a: Not-before is inclusive (`nbf <= now`) while expiration is exclusive (`now < exp`). At `now=20` the token has expired.

practice.name: Build Distributed Systems, The Securitor: first three tasks
practice.locator: First three free tasks of the track, graded in the browser after login
practice.note: Treat a pass as a drill. The section mini-project covers this: a local mTLS or faithful verification mock that checks certificate validity, the matching trust-domain bundle and an allowed SPIFFE ID, then rejects an unknown domain, an expired SVID and a valid but unauthorized ID during bundle rotation.

practice.name: AlgoMaster: Validate JWT Time Claims
practice.locator: `isValid(iat, nbf, exp, now)`; the page tests the inclusive not-before and exclusive expiration boundaries with no clock-skew allowance
practice.note: The page assumes signature verification already happened. State where signature and revocation checks live in your design.

units.stopWhen: Your diagram names every trust boundary with its STRIDE rows, your verification check rejects an unknown trust domain, an expired SVID and a valid but unauthorized ID, and the JWT checks pass including both time boundaries.

fit.note: Coverage failed for a threat-model method: HLD and SPIFFE specify mechanisms but no modeling procedure, so the OWASP cheat sheet fills that gap.

units.title: Authorization on every data path, tenant isolation and multi-tenant fault and restore tests
outcomes: Enforce scoped authorization on every data path, including retry, cache, restore and migration paths.
Isolate tenants with key and predicate discipline, and state which cache entries may be shared across tenants.
Run multi-tenant fault and restore tests that prove one tenant cannot read or mutate another tenant's state.
units.why: A correct happy-path check leaks the moment a retry replays a request, a cache serves a shared entry, or a restore replays another tenant's rows. Isolation is a property of every path, not of one middleware.

next.note: Rotate the credentials those checks depend on.
Propagate tenant-scoped deletion through the same paths.

study.title: Least privilege: small APIs, auditing, breakglass
study.locator: Concepts and Terminology (Least Privilege, Zero Trust Networking); Best Practices (Small Functional APIs, Breakglass, Auditing including Collecting good audit logs); Testing and Least Privilege

study.title: Multi-tenancy: isolation levels and noisy neighbors
study.locator: The three isolation levels; Row-level security as defense-in-depth; Noisy-neighbor defenses; Data residency and crypto-shredding
study.depth: Read for the isolation spectrum and row-level predicates. Skip the bridge-model case study and per-tenant metering as product detail.

study.title: Access models: from ACL to ReBAC
study.locator: AuthZ models: from ACL to ReBAC; Zanzibar and its descendants
study.depth: Read for the model vocabulary only. You implement a local RBAC check in Practice, not Zanzibar.

focus: Derive the tenant predicate from the authenticated identity on each path. A check that runs on ingest but not on restore, retry or cache fill is a second door.
Small functional APIs make authorization auditable: each endpoint takes the identity it needs and nothing more, with breakglass as the named exception.
Cache keys carry the tenant, or the entry is provably tenant-free. A shared entry keyed without the tenant is a cross-tenant read.

Use storage predicates as defense in depth behind endpoint checks. Test both enforcement points, including whether privileged restore roles bypass row-level security; a missing check in either layer must not expose another tenant's rows.
units.reproduce: Without notes, add a tenant predicate to three loglab reads (fresh read, cache fill, restore replay) and state which shared cache entries remain legal and why.
traps: Inheritance flows downward only. The RBAC exercise denies a parent a permission granted to its child; a check that walks the wrong direction grants too much.
Breakglass without audit is a backdoor. The least-privilege chapter pairs every emergency path with logging and review.
Testing with one tenant. A single-tenant test passes vacuously; isolation needs at least two tenants with overlapping keys.

selfTest.q: Roles form the chain 2 inherits 1 inherits 0, with direct masks 4, 2 and 1. What is role 2's effective mask, and does it grant permission bit 1?
selfTest.a: The effective mask is \(4 \mid 2 \mid 1 = 7\), which contains bit 1, so yes. Inheritance accumulates down the chain.

selfTest.q: Role 0 requests a permission granted only to role 2. Granted?
selfTest.a: No. Permissions flow from parent to child, never upward to parents or across to siblings.

selfTest.q: A restore replays rows with the tenant column intact but skips the endpoint check. Is isolation preserved?
selfTest.a: Only if the storage layer re-applies the tenant predicate, for example row-level security, and the restore role does not bypass it. Otherwise the restore path skips the only check.

selfTest.q: Two tenants share a cache entry keyed by query hash without a tenant field. What breaks?
selfTest.a: Tenant A can read tenant B's result. Either scope the key by tenant or prove the entry holds no tenant data.

practice.name: AlgoMaster: Check Effective RBAC Permissions
practice.locator: `hasPermission` with direct bitmasks and parent chains; the page tests downward-only inheritance over acyclic chains
practice.note: Then add the same check to your loglab reads. The section mini-project covers this: multi-tenant fault and restore tests with overlapping keys.

units.stopWhen: Your three loglab reads enforce the same predicate, the RBAC checks pass including the upward-denial case, and a two-tenant test with identical keys shows no cross reads.

fit.note: Least-privilege design, the HLD access models and the Part 5 multi-tenancy chapter cover authorization and isolation; the RBAC drill and the multi-tenant restore tests provide the implementation practice.

units.title: Encryption in transit and at rest, secret and key rotation and audit integrity
outcomes: Wrap data keys with key-encrypting keys and compute the blast radius of any compromised key.
Rotate credentials through a dual-accept overlap without dropping long-lived connections.
Bound metric cardinality and keep audit events tamper-evident against an independently retained checkpoint.
units.why: Keys leak and certificates expire. Rotation and audit bounds decide whether that event is a routine overlap or an outage with unbounded telemetry.

next.note: Verify the backups those keys protect.
Feed rotation and audit events into telemetry with bounded labels.

study.title: Secrets: envelope encryption, dynamic secrets, rotation
study.locator: Where secrets should not live; Envelope encryption and KMS; Dynamic secrets; Leak detection and response
study.depth: Skip Secrets in Kubernetes unless your dossier runs there.

study.title: Certificate lifecycle: rotation and revocation
study.locator: Certificate lifecycle: issuance, rotation, revocation
study.depth: Read only this section here. The handshake and SPIFFE sections belong to the first unit.

study.title: Revocation and key rotation at scale
study.locator: Use an Explicit Revocation Mechanism (Failing open; Revoking credentials at scale); Rotating signing keys
study.depth: Read for the revoke-versus-expire trade-off. Skip firmware rollback constraints.

study.title: Audit logs that answer questions
study.locator: Best Practices: Auditing, with Collecting good audit logs and Choosing an auditor

focus: Compromising a wrapping key exposes its descendants when the attacker also holds the wrapped keys and ciphertext. A plaintext data key can also leak on its own, for example from application memory, without exposing its ancestors or siblings.
Rotation is overlap, not replacement: introduce the new version, accept both, move new connections first, retire the old only after migration.
Revocation is explicit or it is absent. Expiration bounds lifetime; only a deny list or a rotated key stops a live credential now.

Cardinality multiplies. With one series per label combination and every combination present, independent labels with cardinalities 5, 3 and 100 create 1,500 series; in a real audit, count the observed combinations and any per-type series expansion.
units.reproduce: Without notes, write the rotation states (idle, overlap, migrated, retired) with which versions are accepted and emitted in each, and compute the series count for a 5 by 3 by 100 label set.
traps: Retiring the old credential at introduction time. Long-lived clients holding it fail until they reconnect; the overlap exists for them.

Reading fail-open as resilient. The revocation section has nodes enforce their cached revocation list, their last known state, instead of allowing everything when the revocation service is unreachable.
Counting label values instead of their product. Three small labels easily exceed a series budget together.

selfTest.q: Key 1 wraps keys 3 and 4, and records 0 and 1 use those keys. Key 1 is compromised. Which records are exposed?
selfTest.a: Records 0 and 1. The compromised key exposes itself and its descendants; ancestors, siblings and separate trees stay safe.

selfTest.q: Root key 0 of a single key tree is compromised. How many of the tree's five records are exposed?
selfTest.a: All five. The root unwraps every descendant key.

selfTest.q: `beginRotation` fails while a rotation is already active. What state changed?
selfTest.a: None. Failed operations change nothing: the pending version stays pending and acceptance is unchanged.

selfTest.q: Labels with cardinalities 5, 3 and 100 must fit 15 series. Which label goes first?
selfTest.a: The 100-cardinality label. Removing it leaves \(5 \times 3 = 15\) series. Drop larger factors first.

practice.name: AlgoMaster: Analyze Encryption-Key Blast Radius
practice.locator: `affectedRecords` returns exposed record indexes in ascending input order; the page tests self-plus-descendant scope
practice.note: The exercise analyzes key scope only. State where your design holds the wrapped keys and ciphertext it assumes.

practice.name: AlgoMaster: Rotate Credentials Without Downtime
practice.locator: `beginRotation`, `versionForNewConnections`, `accepts`, `completeRotation`; the page tests that failed operations change no state

practice.name: AlgoMaster: Control Metric Label Cardinality
practice.locator: `seriesCount` is the raw product; `labelsToDrop` removes the fewest labels, larger factors first, names returned alphabetically
practice.note: Counting series does not bound audit volume or prove integrity. The section mini-project covers this: redact audit events, persist them in a tamper-evident chain with an independently retained checkpoint, and test record edits, deletion, truncation and restore against that checkpoint.

units.stopWhen: You derive a subtree exposure by hand, your rotation passes the failed-operation cases, a 5 by 3 by 100 label set fits its budget by dropping the right label, and your audit verifier rejects edited and truncated histories against the retained checkpoint.

fit.note: HLD secrets and certificate sections plus the recovery book's revocation and rotation sections cover keys at implement depth, the least-privilege chapter's auditing sections cover audit logs, and three AlgoMaster problems check the arithmetic; audit integrity runs in the section mini-project.

units.title: SLIs, SLOs, error budgets, telemetry and incident reconstruction
outcomes: Define SLIs, SLOs and error budgets with explicit windows, and convert budget burn into alert thresholds.
Emit traces, metrics and logs with W3C context propagation and bounded attributes.
Reconstruct an incident from stored telemetry without assuming synchronized clocks.
units.why: Budgets turn reliability arguments into arithmetic, and propagated context turns scattered logs into one causal trace. Both are prerequisites for every measurement later in this section.

next.note: Turn saturation signals into capacity and shedding policy.
Turn latency and error signals into retry and cascade policy.

study.title: Service level objectives: terminology and practice
study.locator: Service Level Terminology; Indicators; Objectives; Agreements; Indicators in Practice (Aggregation, A Note on Statistical Fallacies); Objectives in Practice (Defining Objectives, Choosing Targets)

study.title: Implementing SLOs: windows and decisions
study.locator: Getting Started; Choosing an Appropriate Time Window; Decision Making Using SLOs and Error Budgets

study.title: Burn-rate alerting
study.locator: Alert on Burn Rate; Multiple Burn Rate Alerts; Multiwindow, Multi-Burn-Rate Alerts
study.depth: Read for the two-window structure. The Systems unit on SLIs, SLOs, error budgets and recovery objectives already derived the single-window budget; do not redo it.

study.title: Monitoring: the four golden signals
study.locator: The Four Golden Signals; Symptoms Versus Causes; Black-Box Versus White-Box
study.depth: Read for signal choice and cause-versus-symptom discipline. Leave Google-internal tooling as examples, not setup.

study.title: Context propagation: traceparent, inject and extract
study.locator: Context; Propagation (default W3C TraceContext propagator); the traceparent field order version, trace id, parent id, flags; Inject and extract; Security best practices (Baggage) (page read 2026-10-15)

study.title: Gray failure: when the detector disagrees with clients
study.locator: Gray versus fail-stop framing; differential observability (Table 1); the stuck handler with a live heartbeat
study.depth: Read as failure-model vocabulary for why reconstruction needs several signals. The cases are Microsoft-internal, not reproducible.

focus: An SLO without a window is not measurable. The Workbook chooses the window before the target, because the same ratio burns differently over 1 hour and 30 days.

Multiwindow burn-rate alerts require the threshold in both a long and a short window. The long window establishes significant budget consumption; the short window confirms the burn is still active and clears the alert soon after recovery.

Propagation carries trace id and parent id in `traceparent`. Correlation needs no synchronized clocks, only the carried parent link. A gray fault bounds what one trace proves: the detector may see healthy while clients see sick, so reconstruction needs several signals.
Baggage is not a secret channel. OpenTelemetry warns against credentials, keys and PII in baggage because it crosses service boundaries and lands in logs.
units.reproduce: Without notes, compute the 30-day error budget in minutes for a 99.9% SLO on a time-based availability SLI, and the nearest-rank p50, p95 and p99 of `[12, 45, 33, 21, 90, 8, 67, 54, 29, 71]` ms.
traps: Averaging percentiles across services. A p99 of p99s is not the system p99; aggregate the underlying samples or count budget burn per service.
Interpolating a nearest-rank percentile. The method returns an observed sample at rank \(\lceil pn/100 \rceil\), never a value between samples.
Alerting on every firing evaluation. The alert manager groups by fingerprint and repeats only after the interval; resolution clears the incident.

selfTest.q: For a time-based availability SLI, how many minutes of full unavailability exhaust a 99.9% SLO over 30 days?
selfTest.a: \(0.001 \times 30 \times 24 \times 60 = 43.2\) minutes. A request-based SLI budgets failed requests instead; converting to minutes needs a traffic assumption.

selfTest.q: Ten samples sort to `[8, 12, 21, 29, 33, 45, 54, 67, 71, 90]`. What are the nearest-rank p50 and p95?
selfTest.a: p50 uses rank \(\lceil 50 \times 10 / 100 \rceil = 5\), value 33. p95 uses rank \(\lceil 9.5 \rceil = 10\), value 90.

selfTest.q: Why do burn-rate alerts use two windows instead of one fast window?
selfTest.a: An alert fires only when both windows exceed the burn threshold. The long window shows the budget is really being consumed; the short window shows the burn is still happening, so the alert clears soon after the errors stop.

selfTest.q: A downstream log carries the trace id from an incoming `traceparent`. Why does that correlation need no clock sync?
selfTest.a: Causality comes from the carried parent link, not from comparing timestamps. Display order may still mislead across machines.

selfTest.q: An alert fires, resolves, then fires again 1 unit later with repeat interval 10. How many notifications?
selfTest.a: Two. Resolution clears the fingerprint, so the next firing is a new incident, not a repeat.

practice.name: AlgoMaster: Calculate Nearest-Rank Latency Percentiles
practice.locator: `latencyPercentiles` returns `[p50, p95, p99]` by 1-based nearest rank without interpolation and without mutating the input

practice.name: AlgoMaster: Deduplicate Alert Notifications
practice.locator: `notificationStates` groups by fingerprint, repeats only after the interval, and clears on resolution; the page tests that a post-resolution firing notifies fresh
practice.note: The section mini-project covers this: inject an incident on the instrumented path, reconstruct its causal request and fault history from stored telemetry with deliberately skewed display timestamps, and mark gaps where instrumentation cannot establish order.

units.stopWhen: Your budget arithmetic and percentile ranks match the worked numbers, you can set a two-window burn alert plus a `traceparent` instrumented path on loglab, and your incident reconstruction marks every gap in the causal order.

fit.note: SRE objectives, Workbook windows and burn-rate alerts, the four golden signals and OTel propagation cover budgets, telemetry and reconstruction at explain and measure depth.

units.title: Capacity headroom, failure reserve, overload detection and load shedding
outcomes: Derive headroom and failure reserve from workload, replication and recovery costs.
Detect overload from queue, latency and saturation signals and shed load early with explicit rejection.
Bound every queue so overload produces backpressure or drops, never unbounded growth.
units.why: Capacity is the difference between a failure you survive and one you join. Headroom arithmetic plus early shedding keeps one slow dependency from queueing the whole system.

next.note: Cap the retries that turn overload into a cascade.
Prove the bounds in the load and chaos campaign.

study.title: Handling overload: limits and client-side throttling
study.locator: Per-Customer Limits; Client-Side Throttling (Client request rejection probability); Criticality; Utilization Signals; Deciding to Retry
study.depth: Read for the throttle-at-the-client argument. Leave datacenter-scale load balancing as background.

study.title: Degradation: tiering, shedding, kill switches
study.locator: Critical-path tiering; Load shedding; Feature flags as kill switches; Cached and static fallbacks

study.title: Capacity: planning math and scaling lag
study.locator: Picking the right signal; Scaling lag: the hidden enemy; Capacity planning math; The dependencies that do not scale
study.depth: Read for the math and the lag warning. Skip the Kubernetes autoscaling family and the Netflix case study unless your dossier runs there.

focus: Headroom is derived, not chosen. Three equal nodes that must survive one failure sustain at most two thirds of total capacity, because each survivor absorbs half the load.
Shed at the client before queues build at the server. Server-side queues hide overload until every layer is full at once.

The Systems unit on Little's Law, capacity and queueing approximations taught \(L = \lambda W\) for stable long-run averages; it does not bound individual waits. Bound queue length to cap backlog, and bound service delay or enforce deadlines to bound waiting time.
Autoscaling lags the spike. The scaling-lag section is why a provisioned reserve, not a scaling policy, covers the first minutes.
units.reproduce: Without notes, derive the three-node tolerate-one bound as a fraction of total capacity, and compute the bottleneck throughput of a stated three-component fixture by hand.
traps: Reading raw capacity as throughput. A database with 5000 work units per second serves only 2500 requests per second at 2 units each; divide capacity by per-request work and take the smallest ratio.
Draining before admitting. The buffer simulator admits arrivals first and drains second each interval; reversing the order understates the peak backlog.
Carrying drain capacity across intervals. Unused drain does not roll over, so idle intervals do not bank future capacity.

selfTest.q: Three equal nodes of capacity \(C\) each must keep serving total load \(L\) after any one node fails. What is the bound on \(L\)?
selfTest.a: Each survivor takes \(L/2\), so \(L/2 \le C\) and \(L \le 2C\): two thirds of the \(3C\) total.

selfTest.q: API, database and cache capacities are 12000, 5000 and 20000 work units per second, with 1, 2 and 0.5 units per request. What is the throughput bound and which component is the bottleneck?
selfTest.a: The ratios are 12000, 2500 and 40000 requests per second, so the bound is 2500, set by the database at \(5000 / 2\). Every request uses every component, so the minimum ratio wins.

selfTest.q: Why does client-side throttling beat server-side queueing during overload?
selfTest.a: Rejected work at the client never consumes server queues, threads or downstream calls. Server queues only delay the same reckoning while sharing fate across callers.

selfTest.q: A buffer of capacity 5 holds 2 events. Interval arrivals are 8 with drain 3. How many are dropped, and what remains?
selfTest.a: 3 fit, so 5 are dropped. Draining 3 of the 5 buffered leaves 2. Arrivals are admitted before draining, and drops are counted per interval.

practice.name: AlgoMaster: Analyze Capacity Bottlenecks
practice.locator: `maxThroughput` is the minimum capacity-per-work ratio within 1e-5; `bottleneck` breaks exact ties alphabetically
practice.note: The section mini-project covers this: derive capacity separately for foreground requests, replication fan-out, backup, restore and repair, reserve each shared resource for a stated concurrent recovery workload, then compare the predicted bottleneck with an injected node-loss run.

practice.name: AlgoMaster: Simulate Log Pipeline Backpressure
practice.locator: Per interval admit-then-drain order with no drain carryover; the pages test backlog consumption of buffer space

units.stopWhen: Your three-node bound, bottleneck arithmetic and one buffer trace all match hand computation, your resource ledger reserves capacity for the stated recovery workload, and your loglab queues reject explicitly past their bounds.

fit.note: SRE overload throttling plus HLD degradation and capacity math cover headroom, detection and shedding at derive and implement depth, with two checked simulations.

units.title: Retry budgets, circuit breaking, cascading and correlated failure and chaos scenarios
outcomes: Derive worst-case retry amplification across dependency layers and cap it with a budget.
Implement circuit breaking with half-open probing and bulkhead isolation.
Distinguish trigger from sustaining cause in a metastable outage and name the chaos scenarios that reproduce each.
units.why: Retries are load, and load is what the overloaded dependency cannot take. Unbudgeted retries plus a shared fate across callers is how one slow service stops them all.

next.note: Turn the trigger catalog into scheduled chaos scenarios.
Cover the same faults with generator, nemesis and checker roles.

study.title: Cascading failures: overload, retries, deadlines
study.locator: Server Overload; Queue Management; Load Shedding and Graceful Degradation; Retries; Latency and Deadlines (Picking a deadline, Deadline propagation, Bimodal latency); Testing for Cascading Failures

study.title: Resilience: timeouts, retries, breakers, bulkheads, jitter
study.locator: The cascading failure story; Timeouts; Retries; Circuit breakers; Bulkheads; No jitter versus Full Jitter versus Equal Jitter versus Decorrelated Jitter

study.title: Metastable failures: trigger and sustaining effect
study.locator: The metastable pattern (vulnerable state, trigger, sustaining effect); Section 2.1 and Figure 2: a 10-second network outage triggers retry amplification while normal offered load is 280 QPS, and retries sustain 560 QPS after connectivity returns; retry storms and cache-miss avalanches as sustaining effects
study.depth: Read as incident vocabulary and design prompts (retry budgets, shedding). The 7-page toy model illustrates; it does not predict.

study.title: Metastable failures in the wild: incident evidence
study.locator: Section 1 (22 metastable failures from 11 organizations); Table 1 public-source incident rows; Section 2.2 (retry policies as the most common sustaining effect, in more than half the studied incidents)
study.depth: Read as a trigger catalog for chaos scenarios. The sample is public reports, not a failure rate; never quote the retry share as universal.

focus: Amplification multiplies down the stack. One retry at each of four layers turns one user call into \(2^4 = 16\) attempts; the budget caps attempts, not intentions.

Equal jitter spreads synchronized retries: for attempts numbered from zero, `temp = min(cap, base * 2**attempt)` and each sleep is `temp / 2` plus a uniform draw from `0` to `temp / 2`, with an independent RNG per client.
The breaker in the exercise uses timeouts as the probe timer, not as failures: a timeout moves open to half-open, and one trial decides.

Removing the trigger does not end a metastable outage. In the worked example the network recovers but the retry loop keeps load high; only dropping offered load below the model's stable threshold recovers it, and that toy threshold is not a production target.
units.reproduce: Without notes, compute worst-case attempts for 1 retry at each of 4 layers, and the first three equal-jitter sleeps for base 1 s, cap 8 s and seed 7 (`random.Random(7)`).
traps: Counting retries per layer instead of multiplying. 2 retries at each of three layers is \((1+2)^3 = 27\) downstream attempts in the Systems unit's example, not 6.
Treating breaker timeouts as failures. In the simulator a timeout leaves closed-state counts unchanged and only advances open toward half-open.
Confusing trigger with root cause. The incident study separates what pushed the system into the vulnerable state from the retry loop that held it there.

selfTest.q: One retry is configured at each of 4 layers. How many attempts can one user call produce?
selfTest.a: \(2^4 = 16\). Each layer doubles the attempts of the layer above, so budgets must be set against the product.

selfTest.q: Equal jitter, base 1 s, cap 8 s, seed 7: what are the first three sleeps?
selfTest.a: About 0.66 s, 1.15 s and 3.30 s. Each is `temp/2` plus a uniform draw up to `temp/2` with `temp` 1, 2 and 4.

selfTest.q: Events `failure, failure, timeout, success` with threshold 2: what states does the breaker report?
selfTest.a: `closed, open, half_open, closed`. The second failure opens it, the timeout starts one trial, and the successful trial closes it.

selfTest.q: A message fails 3 times with `maxRetries = 2`. Delivered or dead-lettered?
selfTest.a: Dead-lettered. Delivery needs failures at or below the budget; exactly at the budget still delivers, one more does not.

selfTest.q: Load returns to normal but the outage persists. What does the metastable model say to do?
selfTest.a: Break the sustaining loop: shed load, drain the retry backlog, restore cache hit rate. Waiting for the trigger to pass already failed.

practice.name: AlgoMaster: Classify Retry Outcomes
practice.locator: `classify` returns `delivered` for failures within budget and `dlq` beyond it, preserving order without mutating input

practice.name: AlgoMaster: Simulate a Circuit Breaker
practice.locator: `simulate` reports the state after every event; the page tests threshold opening, timeout-driven half-open trials and trial-failure reopening

units.stopWhen: Your amplification product, jitter schedule and breaker trace match hand computation, and your loglab retry policy states its budget as a share of traffic.

fit.note: SRE cascade mechanics, HLD resilience patterns and both metastable papers cover budgets, breaking and correlated failure at implement depth, with two checked simulators.

units.title: Replication versus backup and verified backup and restore
outcomes: Distinguish replication from backup by which failures each survives.
Take base plus WAL backups and restore them to a stated recovery target, and replay a logical log to a target with winner-only semantics.
Verify restores by replaying into an isolated target and checking data, not by trusting the backup job's exit code.
units.why: Replicas copy corruption, deletion and schema mistakes within seconds. Only a tested restore path answers the question the incident will ask: what can you bring back, and how do you know.

next.note: Put recovery-point and recovery-time numbers on the verified restore.
Schedule restores as recurring chaos scenarios, not one-off checks.

study.title: Base backup and WAL replay
study.locator: 10.1 Base Backup (`pg_backup_start`, `pg_backup_stop`, `pg_basebackup`, Backup Manifest Files) (page read 2026-10-15)

study.title: How point-in-time recovery works
study.locator: 10.2 How PITR Works (REDO start from the `backup_label`, `restore_command`, `recovery_target_time`, commit versus abort record handling) (page read 2026-10-15)

study.title: Where recovery stops and what verification proves
study.locator: Section 19.5.6 Recovery Target: `recovery_target_lsn` and `recovery_target_inclusive`; then the `pg_verifybackup` reference (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/app-pgverifybackup.html) on what manifest checks cannot cover

study.title: Design for recovery: what you recover from
study.locator: What Are We Recovering From (Random, Accidental, Software and Malicious errors); Design Principles for Recovery (go as quickly as possible, guarded by policy)
study.depth: Read for the failure categories that backups must cover. The revoke and rollback sections belong to the rotation and migration units.

focus: Replication answers node death; backup answers data death. A second replica replays the bad delete just as faithfully as the good write.

In the practice simulator, replay only transactions committed by the inclusive target LSN. PostgreSQL instead redoes physical WAL through the recovery target, and MVCC with transaction status keeps uncommitted effects invisible. Do not equate the two.

Keep and verify the backup manifest when there is one: it detects missing or changed files. A manifest is not required for full-backup recovery and does not replace an isolated test restore with data checks.
Design for the incident categories first: random, accidental, software and malicious errors each stress a different part of the restore path.
units.reproduce: Without notes, write the base-backup plus WAL-archive restore sequence, and state which of two transactions (one committed before the target, one still open at it) leaves effects.
traps: Promoting a standby and calling it a restore test. Failover exercises replication, not the backup chain; the WAL archive may have been broken for months.

Replaying past the target. In the exercise, records at the target LSN apply and records after it do not, so a commit at the target makes its transaction a winner. In PostgreSQL, set the target and `recovery_target_inclusive` explicitly.
Trusting the backup job's success status. Verification means replaying into an isolated target and reading the data back.

selfTest.q: A bad `DELETE` commits and replicates to all standbys. Does failover recover the rows?
selfTest.a: No. Replication copies the delete. Only a backup from before the commit, replayed to a point before it, brings the rows back.

selfTest.q: Transaction 1 commits before the target LSN and transaction 2 is still open at it. Which effects survive recovery?
selfTest.a: Only transaction 1's. In the simulator, winners need a commit record at or before the target and every operation of the open transaction is ignored. PostgreSQL redoes the physical WAL to the target, and transaction status keeps the open transaction's rows invisible.

selfTest.q: What does the backup manifest add, and what does it not prove?
selfTest.a: It lists the backup's files with checksums, so `pg_verifybackup` can detect missing or changed files. It cannot run every check a live server would, so a test restore with data checks is still required.

selfTest.q: Which incident category does a tested restore address that RAID and replicas do not?
selfTest.a: Accidental and malicious errors: mistaken or hostile writes that the storage layer and replicas faithfully preserve.

practice.name: AlgoMaster: Replay WAL to a Point in Time
practice.locator: `recover` replays winner puts and deletes in increasing LSN order and returns rows sorted by key; the page tests that uncommitted transactions leave no effect
practice.note: The section mini-project covers this: take a base backup and WAL archive, restore into an isolated target, and verify committed data, tenant predicates and the current deletion policy.

units.stopWhen: Your simulator handles the winner set, and an isolated restore from your own backup and WAL passes data and policy checks.

fit.note: PostgreSQL base backup and PITR, the recovery-target and verification references and the recovery design principles cover replication versus backup at implement depth; the simulator checks winner logic and the mini-project runs the real restore.

units.title: Recovery point and time objectives and disaster-recovery failover and failback
outcomes: Derive RPO from archive cadence and shipping lag under stated assumptions, and RTO from detection, decision, restore, verification and switch time.
Plan failover and failback across timeline forks: fence the old primary, preserve its divergent writes, and rejoin it by rebuild or `pg_rewind`.
Run a fenced failover and failback drill that records each RTO stage, counts lost acknowledged writes and names both timeline fork points.
units.why: Objectives without a derivation are wishes. RPO and RTO decompose into measurable stages, and the timeline history is what lets the old primary rejoin instead of becoming a split brain. The Systems unit on SLIs, SLOs, error budgets and recovery objectives derived series and parallel availability; here the new work is the failover and failback mechanics.

next.note: Measure the recovery stages under scheduled failover faults.
Feed measured restore times back into the RTO derivation.

study.title: Timelines: failover forks and rejoining history
study.locator: 10.3 timelineId and Timeline History File (timelineId, Timeline History File); 10.4 PITR with Timeline History File (page read 2026-10-15)
study.depth: Read for why promotion forks a timeline and what the history file records. Leave 10.5 Incremental Backup for later.

study.title: Rejoining a diverged primary
study.locator: `pg_rewind`: Description (timeline divergence, the clean-shutdown and `wal_log_hints` or data checksum prerequisites) and the warning on failures while rewinding
study.depth: A fresh base backup is the fallback when the prerequisites do not hold.

study.title: Recovery principles: speed, time and rollback trade-offs
study.locator: Design Principles for Recovery (Design to Go as Quickly as Possible; Limit Your Dependencies on External Notions of Time; Rollbacks Represent a Tradeoff Between Security and Reliability)

focus: RPO counts data, RTO counts time. If every WAL segment closes within 15 minutes, ships to durable storage within 5 more, and the base backup plus WAL chain is intact, recoverable data is at most 20 minutes old; measure and alert on each assumption.

Promotion forks the timeline and the history file records the fork point. The old primary still holds a divergent tail: fence it before promotion, preserve those writes for reconciliation, then rebuild it or run `pg_rewind` before it follows the new timeline.
Failback is a second failover with the same stages: detect, decide, replay, verify, switch. Skipping verification repeats the original incident in reverse.
Failback promotes again, so a round trip forks the timeline twice. Record both fork points and the acknowledged writes that asynchronous failover may have lost.
units.reproduce: Without notes, derive the RPO bound for a 15-minute archive cadence with 5-minute shipping lag and state its assumptions. Then write the failover and failback runbook for one primary and one standby with the fence step, both timeline fork points and the RTO stage each step belongs to.
traps: Promising zero RPO on asynchronous replication. Only synchronous acknowledgement bounds data loss; async always risks the unsent tail.
Rejoining the old primary without the timeline history. Two writers on divergent timelines is a split brain wearing a recovery badge.
Treating a nominal RPO as a promise. A failing archive command stalls shipping while WAL piles up; alert when the newest archived segment ages past the bound.

selfTest.q: WAL archives close every 15 minutes and ship within 5 more. What RPO can you state, and on what conditions?
selfTest.a: At most 20 minutes of writes, provided segments really close on schedule, shipping meets its bound, and the base backup plus WAL chain has no gaps. Restore speed affects RTO, not RPO.

selfTest.q: Detection takes 2 minutes, the decision 5, restore 30, verification 10 and the switch 1. What is the RTO, and which stage do you shrink first?
selfTest.a: 48 minutes. Restore dominates, so a faster restore or a warm standby buys the most; skipping verification saves 10 minutes at the risk of repeating the incident.

selfTest.q: A failover and a later failback both promote a server. How many timeline forks does the round trip create?
selfTest.a: Two. Each promotion starts a new timeline, and each history file records its own fork point.

selfTest.q: After failover, the old primary returns with unreplicated writes. What must happen before it rejoins?
selfTest.a: It stays fenced. Preserve its divergent writes for reconciliation, then rebuild it or run `pg_rewind` with its prerequisites so it follows the new timeline as a standby. It must never write the old timeline again.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: a fenced failover and failback drill on two local PostgreSQL instances or your loglab replicas that records detection, decision, restore, verification and switch times, counts lost acknowledged writes and names both timeline fork points.
units.stopWhen: Your RPO derivation states its assumptions, and your failover and failback drill records every RTO stage, counts lost acknowledged writes and names both fork points.

fit.note: PostgreSQL timelines, `pg_rewind` and the recovery principles cover objectives, failover and failback at derive and measure depth; the drill runs in the section mini-project, and availability arithmetic stays with the Systems unit.

units.title: Rolling protocol and schema evolution, mixed-version behavior and feature gates
outcomes: State backward and forward compatibility for each mixed reader and writer pair in a rolling upgrade.
Roll flags and versions out to a stable slice of subjects with deterministic sticky assignment.
Gate a cutover on ordered readiness checks with drain accounting and a valid rollback.
units.why: Deploys are mixed-version states, not instants. Every pair of old and new code that can meet must already agree on the wire format, and every subject must land on the same side twice in a row.

next.note: Extend the rollout contract to state and storage migration.
Apply the same compatibility directions to your versioned framed RPC.

study.title: DDIA 2e Chapter 5: compatibility directions
study.locator: Chapter 5, Encoding and Evolution: backward and forward compatibility definitions (p. 162); Avro reader-writer compatibility (pp. 174-175); Dataflow Through Databases (pp. 178 to 179); Data encoding and evolution for RPC (p. 186)

study.title: Deployments: rolling, blue-green, canary, flags
study.locator: Deploy vs release; Rolling deploys; Blue-green; Canary with automated analysis; Feature flags as the release control plane
study.depth: Read for the strategy mechanics. Leave Database migrations and expand-contract to the next unit.

focus: Name the writer and reader versions in each direction. New-writer with old-reader needs forward compatibility; old-writer with new-reader needs backward compatibility.
Deploy is not release. A flag separates shipping code from exposing behavior, so a bad release rolls back by flipping the flag, not by redeploying.
Compute the deterministic bucket from the same subject ID on every request. Fresh random assignment, or changing the hash algorithm, salt or subject identity, can flip users mid-rollout.
A rolled-back cutover is valid but incomplete: green stays deployed and switchable, and blue retires only after every old connection drains.
units.reproduce: Without notes, state the compatibility direction each mixed pair needs when a rolling upgrade adds an optional field, and compute bucket and enablement for two user IDs under the sticky hash at 50%.
traps: Testing only new-to-new pairs. Mixed pairs are the rollout: the old reader that chokes on the new field is the outage.
Relying on an unspecified built-in hash. For the exercise's printable-ASCII IDs, start with `h = 0` and update `h = (h * 31 + ord(c)) & 0xFFFFFFFF` for each character `c`; the bucket is `h % 100`.
Retiring blue before drains finish. The cutover auditor keeps blue until green is active and every pre-existing connection has closed.

selfTest.q: A rolling upgrade adds an optional field. Which direction does a new-writer with old-reader pair need?
selfTest.a: Forward compatibility: the old reader must handle data from the newer writer, for example by ignoring the unknown field.

selfTest.q: Which direction does an old-writer with new-reader pair need?
selfTest.a: Backward compatibility: the new reader handles older data, supplying a default for the missing field when the encoding requires one.

selfTest.q: Users land in buckets 40, 17, 9 and 76 at a 50% rollout. Who gets the feature?
selfTest.a: Buckets 40, 17 and 9. Enablement is `bucket < 50`; bucket 76 waits.

selfTest.q: A cutover switches to green, then rolls back to blue. Is the trace valid?
selfTest.a: Valid but incomplete. Rollback to retained blue is legal; completion additionally needs green active with blue retired and drained.

practice.name: AlgoMaster: Build Sticky Feature-Flag Buckets
practice.locator: `bucket` implements the pinned unsigned 32-bit polynomial hash with `h % 100`; `isEnabled` holds exactly when the bucket is below the rollout percent

practice.name: AlgoMaster: Audit a Blue-Green Cutover
practice.locator: Readiness gates must precede the switch, each drain closes one blue connection, and a rolled-back trace stays valid but incomplete

units.stopWhen: Your mixed-pair table names both directions correctly, bucket math matches the pinned hash, and a cutover trace with gates, drains and a rollback audits clean.

fit.note: DDIA compatibility directions plus HLD deployment mechanics cover rolling evolution and gating at explain and implement depth, with bucketing and cutover audits as checked practice.

units.title: Expand, migrate and contract changes, rollback boundaries and migration tests
outcomes: Plan an expand, migrate and contract change with a rollback point in each phase.
Mark irreversible transformations and route them forward instead of rolling back.
Test mixed-version migration with surge and availability limits plus sticky path routing.
units.why: State outlives code, so a deploy that only handles the new shape corrupts the old rows it meets. Expand-contract keeps every intermediate state readable by both versions until no old reader remains.

next.note: Carry version history and lineage through the migration.
Cost the migration traffic and prove the rollback in the campaign.

study.title: Database migrations and expand-contract
study.locator: Database migrations and expand-contract
study.depth: Read this section only here. The rolling, blue-green and canary sections belong to the previous unit.

study.title: DDIA 2e Chapter 5: dataflow through databases
study.locator: Chapter 5, Modes of Dataflow: Dataflow Through Databases (pp. 178-179); Event-Driven Architectures (pp. 189-191), especially preserving unknown fields during republishing
study.depth: Read for mixed-version dataflow and preserving unknown fields; use the HLD migration section for the phased change itself.

study.title: The Migrator: schema and data migration drills
study.locator: First three free tasks of the track (schema migrations, expand and contract, zero-downtime change), graded in the browser after login
study.depth: Treat a pass as a drill. Your evidence is the migration plan and rollback test on your own data.

focus: During expand and migrate, keep every supported reader and writer compatible and keep both representations equal through an atomic update or a tested reconciliation. Contract ends compatibility with old binaries, so document that rollback boundary.
Contract only after the last old reader is gone. Dropping a column while one old binary still selects it turns a cleanup into an outage.

Once the last recoverable original is destroyed by hashing, deletion or lossy recoding, restoring the old shape needs a retained source or backup. A minimum software version stops insecure code rollback; it cannot invert the data transform.
Rolling replacement respects fleet limits: total instances stay within surge, and available capacity never drops below the unavailability bound.
units.reproduce: Without notes, write the three-phase plan for a column rename with the rollback point of each phase, and state which phase a hashing transform can never roll back from.
traps: Migrating before expanding. Backfilling the new column before all writers know it means old writers keep writing the old shape over migrated rows.

Ignoring `maxUnavailable` when stopping old instances. An old instance may stop whenever the remaining ready count stays at least `desiredReplicas - maxUnavailable`; only with `maxUnavailable = 0` must ready replacement capacity come first.
Routing by shortest prefix. The strangler router takes the longest matching prefix, and the `/` rule matches everything as the fallback.

selfTest.q: Where is the rollback point of the migrate phase?
selfTest.a: At the dual-shaped state, before contract. Roll readers back only after verifying the old representation holds every acknowledged write; if new writers updated only the new column, switching back loses those writes.

selfTest.q: A migration hashes raw identifiers into buckets. Why can it not roll back?
selfTest.a: Hashing is irreversible: the bucket does not determine the identifier. Restoring the old shape needs a retained copy of the originals or a backup; otherwise recovery rolls forward with a fix.

selfTest.q: Desired 3, surge 1: how many instances may exist at once, and when may an old instance stop?
selfTest.a: At most 4. An old instance may stop whenever the remaining ready count stays at least `desiredReplicas - maxUnavailable`. With `maxUnavailable = 1` one old instance may stop before any new one is ready; with 0 a ready replacement must come first.

selfTest.q: Rules exist for `/api` at 30% and `/api/v2` at 100%. A request for `/api/v2/orders` from a bucket-80 subject routes where?
selfTest.a: New. The longest prefix `/api/v2` wins over `/api`, and 80 is below 100. Percentage 0 always routes legacy, 100 always routes new.

practice.name: AlgoMaster: Route a Sticky Strangler Rollout
practice.locator: Longest-prefix match with `/` as catch-all; the pinned hash decides buckets and `bucket < rolloutPercent` routes new
practice.note: Then apply the same routing to your loglab migration. The section mini-project covers this: mixed-version migration and rollback tests on existing data.

practice.name: AlgoMaster: Audit a Rolling Deployment Trace
practice.locator: Surge and unavailability limits on every event; unknown events violate; a valid partial trace is not complete

units.stopWhen: Your three-phase plan names every rollback point, both auditors pass including the partial-trace case, and a hashing transform is marked roll-forward-only.

fit.note: HLD expand-contract, DDIA database dataflow and the Migrator drills cover phased migration and rollback at implement depth, with strangler routing and rollout audits as checked practice.

units.title: Data classification, retention, residency and privacy-preserving analytics
outcomes: Classify data into handling tiers with a retention and deletion mechanism per tier.
Map each tier to the jurisdictions that may store and process it, with a transfer rule per border crossed.
Choose a privacy mechanism that matches the question asked, and state what it cannot prove.
units.why: Retention and residency are placement constraints on every store this track built. A log, index or backup that cannot say which jurisdictions hold it, for how long, cannot lawfully or safely hold user data.

next.note: Enforce the retention table with deletion propagation and lineage.
Version the datasets and evaluations the classification covers.

study.title: Residency and erasure: classification, topologies, crypto-shredding
study.locator: Data classification as a distributed-systems problem; Residency topologies; Right-to-erasure and crypto-shredding; Cross-border transfers post-Schrems II; Audit, lineage, and consent

study.title: DDIA 2e Chapter 14: privacy framing
study.locator: Chapter 14, Doing the Right Thing: Privacy and Tracking (pp. 589 to 596)
study.depth: Read for the consent, retention and governance framing only. The chapter argues policy, not mechanisms; every mechanism claim in this unit comes from the HLD chapters and the Systems differential privacy unit.

study.title: Privacy mechanisms: matching primitive to question
study.locator: Differential privacy fundamentals; Federated learning and FedAvg; Choosing the right primitive
study.depth: Read for the mechanism menu. The Systems unit on differential privacy: adjacency, sensitivity, noise and composition already derived that math; do not redo it, and implement nothing here.

focus: Classification is a storage contract: each tier names its retention, its residency and the mechanism that deletes it. A tier without a deletion mechanism is indefinite retention.

Crypto-shredding makes retained ciphertext unreadable only after every usable copy of the decryption keys is destroyed, including cached plaintext keys, key backups and alternate wraps. Plaintext and derived copies need their own erasure.
Residency topologies place the constraint before the data moves. A backup or index copy in another jurisdiction is a transfer, whatever the primary store promises.
Mechanisms answer different questions: noise for aggregate release, federation for training without centralizing data. Neither proves a model forgot its training set.
units.reproduce: Without notes, write a four-tier classification table (tier, retention, residency, deletion mechanism) for loglab data and state the key-destruction condition crypto-shredding depends on.
traps: Deleting the database row and keeping the backups, indexes and telemetry. Erasure must propagate to every copy the lineage records.
Quoting a mechanism as a guarantee. Differential privacy bounds a query release; it says nothing about the raw store beside it.
Treating consent text as residency control. Policies do not place bytes; topologies and transfer rules do.

selfTest.q: A tier keeps raw identifiers for 30 days with per-purpose keys, then destroys the keys while ciphertext remains in cold backup. Is that erasure?
selfTest.a: Only if every usable copy of those keys is gone, including cached plaintext keys, key backups and alternate wraps, and no plaintext or derived copy survives elsewhere. Ciphertext left in backup does not defeat shredding, and shredding alone does not establish legal compliance.

selfTest.q: A replica of the primary store runs in a second jurisdiction. What must the residency mapping add?
selfTest.a: The replica's jurisdiction, the transfer rule covering the border crossed, and matching retention and deletion for the copy. The copy is a transfer even though the application never asked for one.

selfTest.q: Why does this unit implement no privacy mechanism?
selfTest.a: Its job is selection and placement: which tier, which jurisdiction, which mechanism. The Systems units already derived the noise math and demonstrated the attacks; repeating them here teaches nothing new.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: a classification, retention and residency policy table for the dossier's data paths, with the deletion mechanism per tier.
units.stopWhen: Your four-tier table names a verifiable deletion mechanism per tier, every cross-border copy has a transfer rule, and you can say which privacy question each mechanism answers.

fit.note: HLD residency and mechanism chapters plus DDIA governance framing cover classification, residency and mechanism choice at explain depth, with the policy table assigned to the section mini-project.

units.title: Deletion propagation, lineage, provenance and reproducible backfills
outcomes: Propagate deletion past tombstones, caches and derived copies with version watermarks and a durable deletion ledger.
Record lineage from raw source to derived artifact so every copy is reachable from its origin.
Rerun backfills deterministically from pinned inputs, code, configuration, dependencies and randomness.
units.why: Retention tables are promises; propagation keeps them. A delete that stops at the primary while caches, indexes and backfill outputs keep serving the data is erasure theater.

next.note: Apply lineage and snapshot discipline to feature training data.
Version the artifacts the lineage points to.

study.title: Erasure and lineage: crypto-shredding, audit, consent
study.locator: Right-to-erasure and crypto-shredding; Audit, lineage, and consent
study.depth: Read for the erasure mechanisms and lineage requirements. Classification and residency topologies belong to the previous unit.

focus: The Classical ML unit on snapshots, lineage, pipeline serialization and serving parity kept immutable snapshots with per-row lineage, and the LLM Foundations unit on provenance, deduplication and contamination kept raw identity apart from normalized identity. Here the new work is applying both to deletion.

The exercise's cache watermark rejects stale fills at or below the invalidation version, but a newer fill may be accepted. Subject erasure also needs a durable deletion ledger or generation fence that backfills and restores check.

Equal-version puts are idempotent and newer versions must clear the watermark. Allow recreating an erased subject only under an explicit authorization policy, and test a stale source that republishes erased data with a fresh version.

Pin the input snapshot, code, configuration, dependency versions and any randomness or time inputs, and use deterministic ordering. Two reruns must agree under a declared equality policy; if floating-point reductions vary, state and justify a tolerance.
units.reproduce: Without notes, trace a delete from primary through cache watermark to a backfill output, and state the read result when a delayed put at version 6 meets a tombstone watermark at 8.
traps: Expiring the key and resetting its version history. The versioned store keeps version history across expiry and deletion, so a recreated key never reuses an old version number.
Invalidating without a watermark. An event that only removes the cached entry lets an older delayed fill put the data back; the watermark is what makes invalidation idempotent.
Backfilling from live sources. New arrivals during the rerun change the input; snapshot first, then compute.

selfTest.q: A key holds version 5 with watermark 4, and a delayed fill for version 5 arrives. Accept or reject?
selfTest.a: Accept as idempotent: it equals the cached version and sits above the watermark. A fill at version 4 or below would be rejected.

selfTest.q: An invalidation event at version 5 removes the entry, then a delayed put at version 6 arrives. What happens?
selfTest.a: The cache accepts it as the new live value, since version 6 exceeds the watermark of 5, and a delayed put at version 5 would be rejected. If the event was a subject erasure, the deletion ledger must also reject the fresh fill.

selfTest.q: A key expires and is recreated. May it reuse version 1?
selfTest.a: No. Expiration and deletion remove the live entry but keep version history, so the recreated key advances to the next unused version.

selfTest.q: Two backfills of the same date range disagree. What is the first thing to compare?
selfTest.a: Input snapshot identity and code version. Different inputs or different code explain different outputs before any logic bug is suspected.

practice.name: AlgoMaster: Apply Versioned Invalidation Events
practice.locator: Per-key invalidation watermarks with stale-event rejection; the page tests that delayed and duplicate events cannot resurrect invalidated data
practice.note: Then propagate a loglab delete through your own cache watermark. The section mini-project covers this: reproducible backfills from fixed snapshots.

practice.name: AlgoMaster: Build a Versioned TTL Key-Value Store
practice.locator: Expiry at exactly `now + ttl` with monotonic versions across expiry and deletion; `compareAndSet` and `remove` act only on live matching versions

units.stopWhen: Your delete trace names every copy it touches, watermarked invalidation passes the delayed-fill cases, a fresh-version republish of an erased subject is rejected, and two backfills from pinned inputs agree under your declared equality policy.

fit.note: HLD erasure and lineage plus the corpus snapshot and dedup units cover deletion and backfill discipline, with watermarked invalidation and versioned expiry as checked practice.

units.title: Point-in-time feature joins and online and offline feature equivalence
outcomes: Join features to entity rows as of each row's event time with TTL bounds, by hand on a small fixture.
Exclude backfilled values that were not yet available at prediction time with created-timestamp filtering.
Test that the online path serves the same values the offline join produced for the same entity and time.
units.why: Training on a feature value the model could not have seen at prediction time is future leakage with infrastructure. The join rule is what keeps offline metrics honest about online behavior.

next.note: Version the feature service and dataset the join produces.
Retest the joined data against the leakage taxonomy before any model consumes it.

study.title: Point-in-time joins: entity frames, TTL, created timestamps
study.locator: The entity dataframe and `get_historical_features` call; the TTL backward scan (TTL is relative to each entity timestamp, not to query time); the joined result with its two unjoined rows; Retrieving features as of the event time (`filter_by_created_timestamp`, NULL created timestamps excluded); Feast v0.66-branch documentation (page read 2026-10-15)

study.title: Feature retrieval: historical versus online paths
study.locator: Event timestamp (upper bound, inclusive; leakage without it); Retrieving historical features; Retrieving online features (`get_online_features` takes entity rows without timestamps); Feature Services (one service per model version) (page read 2026-10-15)

focus: Each entity timestamp is an upper bound, inclusive. The join takes the latest feature row at or before it, scanning back at most the TTL. This is the mechanical fix for the future leakage in the Classical ML unit on leakage: target, future, entity, duplicate, preprocessing and feedback.

TTL is relative to each entity timestamp, not to query time. Reproducible results also need a pinned feature-source snapshot and join definition, since later backfills can change a retrieval; filter on availability time to reproduce what could have been served then.
Corrections and backfills carry a created timestamp. Without the filter flag, a value corrected after prediction time still joins into training.

Online serving returns the latest value with no timestamp argument. Version the feature definitions both paths use, log the served vector with its materialization state, and compare it with the historical join under the same snapshot, transforms, TTL and availability-time rules.
units.reproduce: Without notes, with TTL 25, join feature rows `(1, 10, 'a', 10)`, `(1, 20, 'b', 20)`, `(1, 28, 'b2', 40)`, `(1, 35, 'c', 35)` (entity, event time, value, created) to entity rows `(1, 12)`, `(1, 30)`, `(1, 65)`, `(2, 10)` (entity, event time). Then repeat with created-timestamp filtering.
traps: Joining the latest feature row regardless of the entity time. The `(1, 30)` row must never see the value from event time 35.
Enabling the created filter with NULL created timestamps. The docs exclude those rows instead of treating them as always available.
Comparing online output to a retrained offline join after a backfill. Equivalence is checked against the stored training frame, not a fresh recomputation.

selfTest.q: Default join: what does each entity row get?
selfTest.a: `(1, 12)` gets `'a'`; `(1, 30)` gets `'b2'`; `(1, 65)` gets nothing, since \(65 - 35 = 30 > 25\); `(2, 10)` gets nothing, since entity 2 has no rows.

selfTest.q: With created-timestamp filtering, what does `(1, 30)` get, and why?
selfTest.a: `'b'`. The `'b2'` row was created at 40, after the entity time 30, so it is excluded and the join falls back to the row from event time 20.

selfTest.q: Why does the TTL miss on `(1, 65)` not depend on when the query runs?
selfTest.a: TTL measures back from each entity timestamp: \(65 - 35 = 30 > 25\) whenever the query runs. Query time never enters the join.

selfTest.q: The online path serves `'c'` for entity 1 while the stored training frame for a `(1, 30)` row holds `'b'`. Is that a serving bug?
selfTest.a: Not by itself: online serves the latest value and time has passed. Compare the logged online vector with the historical join under the same snapshot, transforms, TTL and availability-time rules; a mismatch there is the bug signal.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: a reduced feature-store path with point-in-time joins on a hand-checkable fixture, TTL and created-timestamp cases, and an online versus offline equivalence test.
units.stopWhen: Your hand join matches the stated answers for both flags, and you can say for any served value which entity time and filter produced it.

fit.note: Coverage failed for feature joins: no pool resource teaches them, so the Feast concepts pages fill the gap beside the leakage unit, with join practice assigned to the section mini-project.

units.title: Model-registry state, artifact checksums, retrieval-index freshness and dataset version identity
outcomes: Promote and roll back model versions through registry aliases with lineage to the producing run.
Verify artifacts and checkpoints by checksum before serving or evaluating them.
Build immutable retrieval-index generations from a recorded input frontier and switch readers between them atomically.
Give every dataset and evaluation input a content identity independent of its path.
units.why: A model version, a dataset path and an index name are pointers, and pointers move. Lineage plus checksums plus watermarks turn them into identities a later audit can resolve.

next.note: Feed the versioned dataset back into point-in-time training frames.
Prove rollback and rebuild timing in the campaign.

study.title: Model Registry: versions, lineage, aliases, stages
study.locator: Why Model Registry (version control, lineage and traceability); Concepts (annotations and descriptions); Model Registry in practice (aliases such as @champion, stages, tags)
study.depth: Stages are deprecated since MLflow 2.9 (Model Registry Workflows, Migrating from Stages); use aliases and tags. Page read 2026-10-15.

study.title: Dataset identity: checksum sidecars and pipeline locks
study.locator: `dvc add`, Description and Example: Single file, for `.dvc` content-hash sidecars; for pipeline definition and lock state, the `dvc.yaml` page with its `dvc.lock file` section (https://doc.dvc.org/user-guide/project-structure/dvcyaml-files); for transfer, https://doc.dvc.org/command-reference/push and https://doc.dvc.org/command-reference/pull (page read 2026-10-15)

study.title: Serving versions: feature services and materialize refresh
study.locator: Feature Services (one service per model version); Retrieving online features; Pre-computed feature vectors (rebuilt on `materialize` and `materialize-incremental`) (page read 2026-10-15)
study.depth: Read as the serving-state pattern: named feature groups and refreshed vectors. Feast defines no global input-offset snapshot; the build frontier and the generation swap are your own design. The join mechanics belong to the previous unit.

focus: An alias resolves to a version, and a version resolves to its producing run. Treat registered artifact bytes and run identity as immutable by policy; tags, descriptions and aliases may change under audit.

Record trusted artifact and dataset-content digests with the code commit, configuration, dependencies, seeds and execution inputs. Read the dataset digest from the `.dvc` output entry, not the hash of the sidecar file; hashes verify inputs, and only a rerun shows reproducibility.

Say whether your build metadata is a completeness frontier or an exact snapshot boundary. A completeness watermark through offset 1000 guarantees inclusion through it but may allow newer visible writes; only an immutable build capped at offset 1000 with an atomic generation switch excludes later writes. Partitioned inputs need a per-partition frontier.
DVC tracks content, git tracks the pointer. The small `.dvc` file commits to git while the bytes live in cache or remote; `pull` restores exactly the committed bytes.
units.reproduce: Without notes, resolve `@champion` before and after a promotion and a rollback, and list what an evaluation rerun must match: artifact and dataset-content digests, code commit, configuration, dependencies and seeds.
traps: Versioning the pointer file but not fetching the bytes. A `.dvc` sidecar without `pull` reproduces the hash of data you do not have.
Reading index freshness from wall-clock age. Staleness is measured against the build's input frontier: which writes are included, not how old the files are.
Confusing copying bytes with promoting a registry version. Move the serving alias to the verified version and keep its producing-run identity; byte-identical copies keep the same content identity.

selfTest.q: `@champion` points at v3, then v4 is promoted, then rolled back. What does `@champion` resolve to at each step?
selfTest.a: v3, then v4, then v3 again. Promotion repoints the alias; rollback repoints it back. Neither step rewrites v3 or v4 or their lineage.

selfTest.q: An evaluation reruns with the same dataset path but a different `.dvc` hash. Is it the same evaluation?
selfTest.a: No. Identity is the content hash, not the path. Different bytes mean a different input even under the same filename.

selfTest.q: An index build records a completeness watermark through offset 1000, and offset 1042 just committed. Which rows may a served query reflect?
selfTest.a: Every row through offset 1000, and possibly some newer ones: a completeness watermark is a lower bound. Only an immutable generation capped at offset 1000 with an atomic switch excludes offset 1042.

selfTest.q: A recreated registry key reuses version number 2 after v2 was deleted. What breaks?
selfTest.a: Lineage: two different artifacts claim one identity, and old references to v2 become ambiguous. Versions are append-only; the versioned store in the deletion unit keeps history across expiry for the same reason.

practice.name: AlgoMaster: Build a Versioned TTL Key-Value Store
practice.locator: Monotonic versions per key across expiry and deletion; `compareAndSet` and `remove` act only on live matching versions
practice.note: Treat versions as append-only registry discipline in miniature. The section mini-project covers this: build immutable retrieval-index generations from an identified dataset and per-partition offset frontier, verify document counts and deletions against an independent reference, publish a generation pointer atomically, and test a crash before and after publication plus rollback to a retained generation.

units.stopWhen: You resolve alias moves without touching versions, list every input an evaluation rerun must match, and say for any served read which generation and frontier it came from.

fit.note: Coverage failed for registry, artifact and dataset identity: no pool resource teaches them, so the MLflow, DVC and Feast serving pages fill the gap, with registry practice in the section mini-project.

units.title: A load, chaos, backup and restore campaign with capacity, recovery and migration costs
outcomes: Run a scheduled campaign of load, fault, backup and restore scenarios with named triggers and abort conditions.
Measure SLO impact, recovery point and time, backlog and cost on every scenario.
Keep raw histories with evidence labels that separate simulated, local and inferred claims.
units.why: Every unit in this section feeds this campaign. One compound incident, run on schedule and reconstructed from stored evidence, turns the separate mechanisms into an operated system.

next.note: Extend the campaign with generator, nemesis and checker roles.
Package the campaign histories as an independent reproduction.

study.title: Chaos: experiment framework and blast radius
study.locator: The Principles of Chaos; The experiment framework; Failure modes to inject; Blast radius control
study.depth: Read for the steady-state, hypothesis and blast-radius structure. Run the experiments on your local processes, not on shared infrastructure.

study.title: Error-path testing: why the campaign starts with faults
study.locator: Introduction and Table 1: 198 user-reported failures across Cassandra, HBase, HDFS, MapReduce and Redis, 48 of them catastrophic; of those, 92% involved mishandled explicitly signaled non-fatal errors and 58% were detectable by simple tests. Section 3.2 and Table 5: 98% of the sampled failures needed at most 3 nodes
study.depth: Read as the priority argument: error paths first, scale later. These are proportions of a 2014 sample, not a bound on your system or a measure of risk your tests remove.

study.title: Cascades: testing until failure and incident response
study.locator: Testing for Cascading Failures (Test Until Failure and Beyond, Test Popular Clients); Triggering Conditions for Cascading Failures (Process Death, Process Updates, New Rollouts)

study.title: Incident corpus: triggers for the scenario list
study.locator: Table 1 public-source incidents as the trigger catalog (retry, scale-up, power loss rows); Section 1 study scope (22 failures, 11 organizations)

focus: Every scenario states steady state, trigger, blast-radius bound and abort condition before it runs. A chaos run without an abort condition is an unplanned outage.

Start with error paths, not scale. In the testing paper's sample most catastrophic failures came from mishandled signaled errors and almost all failures needed at most three nodes; load comes after the handlers are correct.
Triggers come from the incident corpus: retry storms, bad rollouts, process death, cache loss. Each scenario names which catalog row it replays.
Cost rows are measured, not estimated: provisioned capacity, recovery time, migration traffic and backlog per scenario, each labeled with the setup that produced it.
units.reproduce: Without notes, write a chaos-experiment card for loglab (steady-state metric, catalog trigger, blast-radius bound, abort condition) plus the four cost-ledger rows the run must fill.
traps: Running chaos before error-path tests pass. Random faults on broken handlers produce noise, not signal; the paper's order is unit-testable faults first.
Quoting incident counts as rates. 22 failures across 11 organizations describe a sample of public reports, not the probability of your next outage.
Ending the campaign at recovery. The ledger needs cost rows too: capacity held, traffic moved and backlog absorbed, or the next incident cannot be budgeted.

selfTest.q: Why does the campaign test error handlers before running load scenarios?
selfTest.a: In the 2014 sample, 92% of the 48 catastrophic failures involved mishandled explicitly signaled errors and 58% were detectable by simple tests. That motivates testing handlers early; it does not measure how much risk your tests remove.

selfTest.q: A scenario replays a cache-loss row from the incident catalog. What must its card name?
selfTest.a: Steady-state hit rate, the loss trigger, the blast-radius bound (which tenants and traffic share), the abort condition, and the recovery and cost rows to measure.

selfTest.q: Recovery completed but the ledger has no cost rows. Is the scenario done?
selfTest.a: No. Without capacity, traffic and backlog numbers the run cannot be budgeted or compared, so the campaign objective is unmet.

selfTest.q: A fault needs 5 nodes to reproduce. Does that contradict the testing paper?
selfTest.a: No. The paper found that 98% of sampled failures needed at most 3 nodes, not all of them, and its sample already has larger cases. Label the 5-node result by its method: simulated if a simulator produced it, local measured if local processes did.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: the full load, chaos, backup and restore campaign with capacity, recovery and migration cost measurement on loglab.
units.stopWhen: Your campaign runs on schedule with experiment cards, abort conditions, reconstructed histories and a filled cost ledger, and every claim carries its evidence label.

fit.note: HLD chaos structure, the error-path testing paper, SRE cascade testing and the incident catalog cover the campaign and its costs at measure depth, with the campaign itself assigned to the section mini-project.
